name: Raising Hands
baseMeaning: A raising hands emoji: two open hands raised high above the head, fingers spread.
tldr: Raising Hands 🙌: marking celebration, relief, or praise.

contextMeanings.meaning: In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — marking celebration, relief, or praise — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.
The plain reading: two open hands raised high above the head, fingers spread. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: Announcing that a deadline slipped but survived 🙌

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as marking celebration, relief, or praise.
contextMeanings.example: Celebrating a result you barely earned 🙌

contextMeanings.meaning: Used sarcastically it is the gesture with the deadpan delivery: marking celebration, relief, or praise, said without believing any of it.

platformNotes.note: In TikTok comments 🙌 is the fastest way to answer a video without typing anything. The gesture stays marking celebration, relief, or praise, and the tone of the comment underneath it carries the rest.

In Slack 🙌 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for announcing that a deadline slipped but survived, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.
On Discord 🙌 is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its marking celebration, relief, or praise reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.

On X and Twitter 🙌 does most of its work in replies, where it tags a message like celebrating a result you barely earned. Short enough to survive being the whole post, which is exactly why it is used that way.

On iOS the Raising Hands 🙌 renders as the neutral drawing, and the neutral swatch is what most people send without thinking about it. A message like announcing that a deadline slipped but survived is the kind that carries it — the picture lands before the sentence does.

generationalNotes.note: Older senders use 🙌 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the marking celebration, relief, or praise subtext in it.

Gen Z reaches for 🙌 to do the work of announcing that a deadline slipped but survived, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is marking celebration, relief, or praise.

Millennials tend to send 🙌 deliberately, usually for something like celebrating a result you barely earned, and they read marking celebration, relief, or praise into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses 🙌 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read marking celebration, relief, or praise into it than younger senders are.

warnings.title: 🙌 and 🤲 get swapped
warnings.description: The Palms Up Together 🤲 is one tap away in every picker, and it does not carry the same reading — palms up together read as prayer or offering, the raised hands read as noise and celebration. Check which one you actually picked.

warnings.title: The reading it usually gets is not the one it was sent with
warnings.description: People take 🙌 as something else fairly often: it gets assumed to be shared joy when it is often posted as gratitude or as a plea for attention — with no context it usually means "look what happened" rather than applause. The sentence around it is usually what settles the meaning.

seoTitle: 🙌 Raising Hands Emoji Meaning and How to Use It
seoDescription: What 🙌 means when people send it, the raising hands reading, and how to answer it without guessing.

longForm.overview:
What follows is the useful part: the two things the raising hands is actually for (announcing that a deadline slipped but survived and celebrating a result you barely earned), the reading it gets when it is not what the sender meant, and the five tone pages that sit under this one.

There is not a lot to the picture. 🙌 is two open hands raised high above the head, fingers spread, added in Unicode 6.0 and filed under hand. What it does in a message is carry a meaning — here, marking celebration, relief, or praise — without anyone having to write it out.

That plain reading is the one most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one. The picture is doing the same work as the sentence it replaces, and it lands first.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets assumed to be shared joy when it is often posted as gratitude or as a plea for attention — with no context it usually means "look what happened" rather than applause. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 🤲 Palms Up Together: palms up together read as prayer or offering, the raised hands read as noise and celebration. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

There are five tone versions of this emoji, and they are not copies of this page. Each one describes the same gesture from inside a different group, because a tone is read as a signal about the sender before the sentence is read.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
The common uses are announcing that a deadline slipped but survived and celebrating a result you barely earned. The first one is about speed — the picture replaces the explanation, and it lands before the words would have. The second is about tone — the sentence stands on its own, and the emoji is there to change how it reads.

The same emoji in three rooms: a family thread, a work channel, and a dating app. In the first it closes a conversation, in the second it hands something over, in the third it is a joke with an eyebrow raised. The drawing never changes; the expectation of the reader does.

That is also the reason the skin-tone variants are written as their own pages rather than as one page with a table of swatches. A tone is not a setting, and it is read differently.

Look at how often 🙌 is used to avoid typing. A question goes out, a question comes back, and in between there is a single picture standing in for an answer that would have taken a sentence. It reads as "marking celebration, relief, or praise", which is fine until it is not.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Watch the picker, and watch the thread. 🙌 is easy to send when 🤲 Palms Up Together was meant — palms up together read as prayer or offering, the raised hands read as noise and celebration. And the emoji has no business being the whole reply to somebody who has just told you something bad: it reads as "marking celebration, relief, or praise", which is about the gesture rather than about them.

The problem is not the emoji, it is the message underneath it. 🙌 gets assumed to be shared joy when it is often posted as gratitude or as a plea for attention — with no context it usually means "look what happened" rather than applause, and the drift happens silently. Nobody notices that the meaning changed, because the change was in a picture.

Nor is it a good opener with a stranger. The drawing is cold, and raising hands gestures have collected a faintly superior edge from being used to reply to other people for years.

Professional settings are the other place to leave it alone. Put 🙌 next to somebody's performance, or in a first note to a client, and marking celebration, relief, or praise is the note it reads as — a note that costs more in a workplace than in a group chat.
longForm.howToReply:
Matching works when the message was a reaction: send 🙌 back and the tone is confirmed without a word. It does not work when the message was aimed at you. A request, a handover, a nudge — those want a sentence, because two gestures in a row leave the question open.

If you cannot tell how the raising hands was meant, read the line above it instead. 🙌 gets assumed to be shared joy when it is often posted as gratitude or as a plea for attention — with no context it usually means "look what happened" rather than applause; the sentence underneath is the part that disambiguates it.

Warmth needs words next to the picture. Something like announcing that a deadline slipped but survived sent with 🙌 on its own is a coin toss between marking celebration, relief, or praise and something sharper, and the sender never gets to pick which one landed.

faqs.question: What does 🙌 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🙌 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under raising hands show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does 🙌 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 🙌 is used for marking celebration, relief, or praise. The drawing shows two open hands raised high above the head, fingers spread, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🙌 and 🤲?
faqs.answer: Palms up together read as prayer or offering, the raised hands read as noise and celebration. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is 🙌 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as marking celebration, relief, or praise, but it gets assumed to be shared joy when it is often posted as gratitude or as a plea for attention — with no context it usually means "look what happened" rather than applause. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

conversationExamples.message: announcing that a deadline slipped but survived 🙌
conversationExamples.interpretation: Family threads are where this lands most naturally. The reading is marking celebration, relief, or praise, and nobody in the thread is reading it as anything sharper than that.
A public sign-off, with the emoji as the full stop. The picture is doing the punctuation, which is why it is sent instead of a sentence.

conversationExamples.message: announcing that a deadline slipped but survived 🙌
conversationExamples.interpretation: The everyday use: the picture carries the whole line. It lands as marking celebration, relief, or praise, and matching it with the same emoji is a normal reply.

conversationExamples.message: celebrating a result you barely earned 🙌
conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as marking celebration, relief, or praise, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.

conversationExamples.message: there is something you should know 🙌
conversationExamples.interpretation: A small joke or a nudge, with the emoji doing the tone work. It gets assumed to be shared joy when it is often posted as gratitude or as a plea for attention — with no context it usually means "look what happened" rather than applause more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.
